content: Gestation refers to the process of carrying an embryo or fetus within the body of a female viviparous animal. In mammals, pregnancy can involve one or more gestations simultaneously, which is referred to as multiple gestations. According to the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), over 136,000 multiple human births were recorded in the United States in 2003. The duration of a gestation is termed the gestation period, while the amount of time the offspring has spent developing in the uterus is referred to as the gestational age. In humans, pregnancy is divided into three trimesters, each lasting approximately three months. The third trimester begins at around 28 weeks of gestation. A fetus is considered viable at 23 weeks of gestation, meaning it has a chance of surviving outside the womb. However, before this point, critical developmental milestones necessary for survival outside the uterus have not yet occurred. It is important to note that this threshold is somewhat arbitrary, as some infants born before 23 weeks have survived, but only with extensive medical intervention. In humans, childbirth typically occurs between 37 and 42 weeks of gestation. Births occurring before 37 weeks are classified as preterm. A fetus is generally considered viable after 25 weeks of gestation. Preterm births and low birth weight are significant contributors to infant mortality, accounting for approximately 17% of infant deaths. Preterm births alone are responsible for 12% of infant deaths, with the majority (84%) occurring between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation. Globally, it is estimated that two million newborns die annually within the first 24 hours of life. In mammals, pregnancy begins when a fertilized zygote implants into the female's uterus. The pregnancy concludes when the offspring exits the uterus.
